stem: Which quotation from The Gauge at Pell Point most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Gauge at Pell Point is an 1894 novel by Harriet Coyle. Its main character, Nell Ambry, lives in a lighthouse on a rocky coast and keeps the daily weather log that her father began decades earlier. The log records rainfall, wind direction and air pressure for passing ships. Most of the novel takes place over one harsh winter. In an essay on the book, a literary critic claims that Nell keeps her weather records faithfully even when the conditions make the work unpleasant.
choices: "Nell loved the quiet hour after a storm, when the clouds broke apart and the harbor lay still and silver beneath them."
"Her father had kept the logbook for thirty years, and its pages had gone brown and soft from the damp of the tower."
"Though the sleet stung her cheeks and numbed her fingers, Nell climbed to the gauge at dawn and wrote down every figure."
"On mild mornings Nell would linger beside the barometer, idly tapping its glass and humming quietly to herself."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Nell keeps her records faithfully, and she does so even when conditions are unpleasant. In this line the sleet stings and numbs her (unpleasant conditions), yet she climbs to the gauge and records every figure (faithful record-keeping). It is the only choice that shows both parts.

A.why: This line has the right setting and a strong feeling about the weather, but Nell isn't recording anything, and the moment is calm rather than unpleasant. You were drawn by the matching mood and topic, but the line shows neither part of the claim.

B.why: This line describes the logbook and her father's history with it. It is about the right object, but it says nothing about Nell's own diligence or about hard conditions.

D.why: Nell is near the instruments here, but the mornings are mild and she is idling, not recording. This shows only half the claim at most and leaves out the unpleasant conditions entirely.

stem: Which quotation from The Valley Songbook most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Valley Songbook is a 1931 novel by Tomas Varga. It follows Anselm Reiter, a musicologist who spends years collecting folk ballads from mountain villages before they are forgotten. Other scholars in the novel compete to publish first and to have collections named after themselves. Reiter is different. According to one reviewer, Reiter cares more about keeping the songs alive than about receiving credit for collecting them.
choices: Reiter spent whole winters traveling from village to village, his notebook tucked inside his coat against the cold.
"I do not mind if no one recalls who wrote these tunes down," Reiter said, "so long as someone is still singing them."
Reiter was delighted when the city paper printed his portrait above a long article praising his new collection.
The oldest singer in the valley knew forty ballads, each of which she had learned as a girl from her own grandmother.
explanation: The claim compares two things: Reiter values the songs surviving more than he values getting credit. In this line he says he doesn't mind being forgotten (credit doesn't matter) as long as people keep singing the songs (survival matters). That puts both halves of the comparison in one line.

A.why: This shows that Reiter is dedicated to collecting, but it says nothing about credit. This is the half-the-claim trap: the line is about hard work, not about what he values more.

C.why: Here Reiter is delighted by public praise, which suggests he does care about recognition. That works against the claim.

D.why: This line describes a singer and how the songs were passed down. It has the right subject, folk ballads, but tells you nothing about Reiter's attitude.

stem: Which quotation from On the Training of Runners most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: On the Training of Runners is a 1908 book by the track coach Walter Prentiss. At the time, many coaches assumed that athletes improved simply by running as many miles as possible. Prentiss took a different view. Historians of sports science note that he argued rest was just as necessary for a runner's improvement as hard training.
choices: "The runner should eat plain food, take very little sugar, and avoid all rich sauces in the days before a contest."
"No athlete ever won a race by training only when the mood suited him; the work must be done daily, in all weather."
"Sleep is a pleasant indulgence for the idle, but it does nothing to build the strength that a racer truly needs."
"The hard mile and the long sleep are partners in the making of a runner; neglect either one, and he will not improve."
explanation: The claim puts rest and hard training on equal footing as needs for improvement. This line calls the hard mile and the long sleep "partners" and says neglecting either one stops improvement. That shows both elements and their equal importance.

A.why: Diet is related to preparing for a race, but the line mentions neither rest nor training. It is on topic but doesn't address the claim.

B.why: This line stresses daily hard training, which is only one half of the claim. It leaves out rest completely. A quotation that matches part of the claim isn't enough.

C.why: This line says sleep does nothing to build strength, which is the opposite of the view the passage gives Prentiss.

stem: Which quotation from The Pump on Carrow Street most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Pump on Carrow Street is a 1952 play by Muriel Ostrander. It is set in a crowded city neighborhood during a cholera outbreak. The town physician, Dr. Imogen Hale, suspects that a shared public water pump is spreading the disease. The residents distrust her and keep using it. A theater scholar argues that the play presents Hale as someone who keeps warning the public even though her warnings are repeatedly ignored.
choices: HALE: "Every morning I post the notice on the pump, and every afternoon I find it torn down. Tomorrow I will post it again."
HALE: "The water from the northern spring runs clear and cold; I have tested it three times now and found nothing amiss."
HALE: "I have warned them quite enough. If they will not listen to reason, then let them drink whatever they please."
HALE: "Half the families on this street are sick now, and it is the youngest children who are suffering the worst."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Hale's warnings are ignored, and she keeps warning anyway. Her notice is torn down every day (ignored), and she says she will post it again tomorrow (she persists). This line shows both.

B.why: This line is about testing water, so it fits the public-health subject. But it describes a different water source and involves no warnings or resistance from the residents.

C.why: Here Hale gives up on warning people, which is the opposite of the persistence the claim describes.

D.why: This line comes from the right situation and has the urgent tone you might expect, but it only describes the outbreak. It shows no warning and no one ignoring her, so it misses both parts of the claim.

stem: Which quotation from "The Surveyor's Confession" most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: "The Surveyor's Confession" is an 1887 poem by Edwin Marlowe. Its speaker is an aging mapmaker who has spent his life charting a small coastal town. Looking over his finished map, the speaker reflects on what his careful work achieved. In a study of Victorian poetry, one critic claims that the speaker regrets that his map, though accurate, cannot capture the life of the town.
choices: "My ink was black, my paper smooth and fine, / And I worked by candle long into the night."
"I drew each river's bend and every hill, / But not the voices calling down the lane."
"The finished chart held all the town contained— / Its songs, its fires, the faces at the door."
"Beyond the hills there lay a land unknown, / Whose roads no surveyor ever walked."
explanation: The claim has two parts: the map is accurate, and it still fails to capture the town's life. In the first half of the line he drew every bend and hill (accuracy). In the second half he admits the voices in the lane are missing (the life left out). This line shows the full contrast.

A.why: This line shows the speaker working hard on the map, which fits the scene. But it says nothing about what the map leaves out, so the regret half of the claim is missing.

C.why: This line says the map captured everything, including songs and faces. That reverses the claim that the map cannot capture the town's life.

D.why: This line is about unmapped land beyond the town. That is a different limitation, not the one in the claim, which is the map's failure to capture the town's own life.

stem: Which quotation from The Millrace most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: The Millrace is a 1928 novel by Clara Dunmore. It is set in a river valley during a spring when heavy snowmelt swells the stream that drives the local grain mill. The mill's owner, Ezra Pell, knows that the stream can overflow its banks within hours once the thaw begins. Literary critics have noted that in the novel's early chapters, Ezra keeps a close watch on the rising water even while he is busy with his ordinary work: ______
choices: "Ezra had always loved the low sound of the stream, which seemed to him the oldest and steadiest voice in the whole valley."
"Even as he stacked the grain sacks, Ezra glanced every few minutes at the notched post by the millrace, noting how far the water had climbed."
"When the spring water rose, the neighbors down the lane carried their chairs and quilts to the upper rooms and waited for it to fall."
"Ezra finished hauling the grain sacks early that evening and sat out on the porch steps, his mind drifting far from the mill."
explanation: The claim has two parts: Ezra watches the rising water closely, and he does it while busy with his ordinary work. In choice B he is stacking grain sacks (ordinary work) and checking the marked post every few minutes to see how high the water has risen (close watch). It is the only quotation that shows both parts.

A.why: You went with the right mood and vocabulary. Ezra cares about the stream here, but the line shows neither part of the claim. He isn't tracking the water's rise, and he isn't working. Feeling something about the river is a related idea. It isn't the claim.

C.why: You picked a line from the right scene, the rising spring water, but it describes the neighbors. Ezra isn't in it. The claim is about what Ezra does, so a line about other people can't illustrate it.

D.why: You matched only half the claim. Ezra is doing his ordinary work, but then his mind drifts "far from the mill." That is the opposite of keeping a close watch on the water. The line works against the claim instead of supporting it.
